about.title: The Quadratic Formula and the Discriminant
audience: anyone who wants to go slowly and check each step
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. The class has two big ideas, the formula and the discriminant, and each gets its own worked examples. A good place to take a break is after the beat called 'Answers with square roots'. The discriminant starts right after it.

10.3: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula (OpenStax Elementary Algebra 1e)

say.text: Welcome to class 44. Last time you solved quadratics by completing the square. Today you get one tool that handles every quadratic.

show.text: The Quadratic Formula and the Discriminant

say.text: We have two goals. First, solve any quadratic with the formula. Second, tell how many real solutions it has before you solve it.

show.text:
Goal 1: solve any quadratic with the formula
Goal 2: use the discriminant to count real solutions
Bonus: pick the best method for each problem

say.text: First, the starting point. The formula works on a quadratic in standard form, and a can't be zero.

show.text: Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0

say.text: The letters a, b and c are the numbers in front. Look at 2x² + 9x − 5 = 0. The sign stays with its number, so c is negative five.

ask.q: In 2x² + 9x − 5 = 0, what are a, b and c?
ask.why: a is the number with x², b is the number with x, and c is the number on its own. The minus sign belongs to the five, so c = −5.

say.text: Now the formula itself. Read it as: negative b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4ac, all over 2a.
The plus-or-minus sign means two answers. One uses plus and one uses minus. The fraction bar covers the whole top part.
Where does it come from? You already know the tool. It is completing the square, done once with letters instead of numbers.

show.text:
Start with ax² + bx + c = 0
Move c to the other side
Divide everything by a
Add (b ÷ 2a)² to both sides
The left side is now a perfect square
Take square roots (± on the right)
Subtract b ÷ 2a: the formula appears

say.text: So the formula is not magic. It is the same steps you used last class, done once for every quadratic.

show.text: The formula = completing the square, done once for all quadratics

ask.q: Which method is the quadratic formula built from?
ask.why: Solving ax² + bx + c = 0 by completing the square, with letters in place of numbers, gives the formula.

say.text: Now let's use it, one step at a time. Step one: standard form. Step two: write down a, b and c. Step three: write the formula.

show.text:
1. Put the equation in standard form
2. Identify a, b and c
3. Write the formula
4. Substitute, using brackets
5. Simplify

say.text: Example: 2x² + 9x − 5 = 0, so a = 2, b = 9, c = −5. Put brackets around every number you substitute. That protects the minus signs.
Do the part under the root first. Nine squared is 81. Then 4 times 2 times negative 5 is negative 40. Subtracting a negative is adding.

ask.why: 4(2)(−5) is −40. Taking away −40 is the same as adding 40, so 81 + 40 = 121.

say.text: The square root of 121 is 11. So x equals negative 9 plus or minus 11, over 4. Now we split it into the plus answer and the minus answer.
Always check. Try x = −5 in the original: 2 times 25 is 50, plus 9 times −5 is −45, minus 5. That is 50 − 45 − 5 = 0. It works.
Next, the most common slip is a negative b. Take x² − 6x + 8 = 0. Here a = 1, b = −6, c = 8. So −b is positive 6, and b squared is (−6)², which is positive 36.

ask.why: b is −6, so −b means the opposite of −6, which is 6.

say.text: Finish it. Under the root: 36 − 32 = 4, and its root is 2. So x = (6 ± 2) ÷ 2. That gives 4 and 2.
Sometimes the equation isn't in standard form yet. Take 3x² = 5x − 2. Do some algebra first to get everything on one side.

ask.q: After moving everything to one side, what are a, b and c for 3x² − 5x + 2 = 0?
ask.why: Read each number with the sign in front of it: +3, −5, +2.

say.text: Finish it: 25 − 24 = 1, and the root of 1 is 1. So x = (5 ± 1) ÷ 6. That gives 1 and 2/3.
Answers with square roots. Sometimes the root isn't a whole number. That is fine, and it can happen with this formula.
Under the root: 16 + 4 = 20. The root of 20 is 2 times root 5. So x = (4 ± 2√5) ÷ 2, and dividing everything by 2 gives 2 ± √5. That is about 4.24 and −0.24.

show.text:
Exact: x = 2 + √5 and x = 2 − √5
Approximately: 4.24 and −0.24

say.text: Nice work. This is a good place for a short break if you want one. Next we look at the part under the square root, because it tells us a lot.
The discriminant is the expression under the square root: b² − 4ac. We give it its own name because it carries a lot of information.
Its sign tells you how many real solutions there are. Positive gives two. Zero gives one. Negative gives none.

show.text:
b² − 4ac > 0  →  2 real solutions
b² − 4ac = 0  →  1 real solution
b² − 4ac < 0  →  0 real solutions

say.text: Why? Because it sits under a square root. A positive number has two roots, a plus one and a minus one. Zero has only one. And a negative number has no real square root.

show.text: Positive: ±√ gives 2 answers. Zero: ±0 gives 1 answer. Negative: no real root.

say.text: A note: the discriminant tells you how many solutions. It doesn't tell you what they are. You still need the formula for that.

show.text: It counts the solutions. It does not find them.

say.text: It also links to the graph. The solutions are where the parabola meets the x-axis, so the count is the number of x-intercepts.

show.text: Three parabolas drawn over one x-axis. Left: a U-shape that crosses the axis in two places, labelled 2 solutions. Middle: a U-shape whose bottom point just touches the axis, labelled 1 solution. Right: a U-shape that floats completely above the axis, labelled 0 solutions.

say.text: Let's test it on two equations from before. For x² − 4x − 1, the discriminant is 20. That is positive, which matches the two answers we found.
Now x² − 6x + 9 = 0. We get 36 − 36 = 0, so just one solution. The formula gives x = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
Your turn. Take x² + 2x + 5 = 0. Find a, b and c, then work out the discriminant.

ask.q: How many real solutions does x² + 2x + 5 = 0 have?
ask.right: None. The discriminant is 4 − 20 = −16, which is negative.
ask.why: b² − 4ac = 2² − 4(1)(5) = 4 − 20 = −16. A negative discriminant means no real solutions. The parabola never touches the x-axis.

say.text: One more use. If the discriminant is positive and a perfect square, like 121 earlier, the answers are tidy fractions. That also means the equation could have been factored.

show.text: Positive and a perfect square → neat answers, and it factors

say.text: That leads to our last topic, choosing a method. The formula always works, but it is not always the quickest.

show.text: Part 3: Which method should I use?

say.text: Try factoring first. If the quadratic factors easily, it is very quick. Next try the square root property, if the equation looks like ax² = k. Use the formula for everything else.

show.text:
1. Try factoring first
2. Square root property if it looks like ax² = k or a(x − h)² = k
3. Quadratic formula for anything else

say.text: Three quick cases. x² = 49 has only an x² term, so square roots. x² − 5x + 6 = 0 factors into (x − 2)(x − 3). And x² + 3x + 1 = 0 has no pair of whole numbers that multiply to 1 and add to 3.

show.text:
x² = 49 → square root property
x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → factoring
x² + 3x + 1 = 0 → ?

ask.q: What is the best method for x² + 3x + 1 = 0?
wrong: Guess and check until it works
ask.why: No whole numbers multiply to 1 and add to 3, so it doesn't factor easily. It also has an x term, so the square root property doesn't fit. The formula always works.

say.text: Now a sports problem. A ball is kicked and its height in feet after t seconds is h = −16t² + 20t + 6. This model is made up for practice. When does it land? Set h to 0.
Under the root: 20² is 400, and 4 times −16 times 6 is −384. So 400 + 384 = 784, and the root of 784 is 28. Then t = (−20 ± 28) ÷ (−32).
Two answers, but time can't go backwards here. The clock starts when the ball is kicked, so −0.25 seconds is before the kick. The ball lands at 1.5 seconds.

ask.q: Why do we throw out t = −0.25 in the ball problem?
ask.right: Time can't be negative here, because the clock starts at the kick
wrong: It fails the check when we substitute it
Negative answers are always wrong in algebra
ask.why: Both numbers solve the equation. We only keep the one that makes sense in the story. In other problems a negative answer can be fine.

say.text: Here are the slips to watch for. People make mistakes with this formula, so slow down and use brackets.

show.text:
Get standard form first
Keep the sign with a, b and c
Use (−6)² = 36, not −36
The fraction bar covers the whole top
Don't forget the ± (two answers)

say.text: Let's recap. The formula solves any quadratic. The discriminant, b² − 4ac, counts the real solutions before you start: two, one or none.
One last check. Suppose you work out b² − 4ac and get 25.

ask.q: If b² − 4ac = 25, how many real solutions are there?
ask.why: 25 is positive, so there are two real solutions. Since 25 is a perfect square, the answers are neat numbers too.

say.text: Well done today. Next class we use quadratics as models, for things like the path of a ball. Rest up, and come back when you're ready.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Babylonian clay tablets already held formulas for problems that lead to quadratics, though not a way to solve the standard one-variable quadratic.

One root of the quadratic formula, with no derivation, appears in Brahmagupta's writings in India. About 200 years later, around 825, the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi solved the general quadratic in an influential work.
Abraham bar Hiyya published Liber embadorum, the first book published in Europe to give the complete solution of the quadratic equation.

other_side.claim: The Babylonians were the first to solve quadratic equations.
other_side.other_view: This is often said, but historians disagree on how far to take it. MacTutor calls it an over-simplification, because the Babylonians had no notion of an equation. Another paper says their tablets show formulas for quadratic-type problems but no way to solve the standard quadratic.

other_side.claim: Brahmagupta gave us the quadratic formula.
other_side.other_view: MacTutor describes his method as almost modern and as allowing negative quantities. A mathematical paper says one root of the formula appears in his writing around 628 without a derivation, and that he did not discover it himself. Credit is shared across many cultures.

other_side.claim: A negative discriminant means the equation has no solutions.
other_side.other_view: In Algebra 1 it means no real solutions. Later courses show that such equations do have solutions in a larger number system called complex numbers.
